newsitem.title: FRANCE: Calls for Juppe's replacement as French RPR head.
newsitem.headline: Calls for Juppe's replacement as French RPR head.

text.p: Several senior members of France's Gaullist RPR party called on Tuesday for defeated ex-prime minister Alain Juppe to be ousted as leader in the start of a potentially vicious power struggle on the shattered political right.

Veteran deputy Pierre Mazeaud, chairman of the outgoing National Assembly's legal committee, said Juppe should be replaced by his arch-rival Philippe Seguin following Sunday's parliamentary election rout.
"Philippe Seguin is the only person who can restore the lost confidence of our members, our voters and France," Mazeaud said in a statement.
"It is clear the RPR cannot simply drive back on to the road with the same driver (Juppe) who has just deliberately crashed 140 deputies into a wall," said parliamentarian Didier Julia.

France 2 television said hardline former interior minister Charles Pasqua, Seguin's partner in the 1992 referendum campaign against the Maastricht treaty on European union, had also demanded that Juppe be removed.

The calls for his replacement followed Monday's resignation of RPR secretary-general Jean-Francois Mancel, who also lost his own parliamentary seat as part of the centre-right's crushing defeat by the Socialist-led left-wing coalition.

"It seems normal that our movement, which will now write a new page in its history, should do so under the leadership of a new team," Mancel wrote to Juppe without making clear if he believed Juppe should also go.

President Jacques Chirac, founder of the RPR, dumped Juppe as premier between the two rounds of the election when it became clear voters saw the vote as a referendum for or against the unpopular prime minister.

Chirac has not taken sides publicly but political sources said he was likely to resist Seguin's efforts to take over the party. Seguin is known to harbour resentement against Chirac for choosing Juppe instead of him as prime minister in 1995.

The burly former National Assembly speaker could well try to use the party machinery to set himself up as a rival or successor to Chirac at the next presidential election in 2002. Chirac is widely assumed to want to stay for a second term.
Seguin was quoted on Monday by L'Est Republicain, the main newspaper serving his east France power base, as forecasting blood on the walls in the fight for control of the party.
The daily said Seguin had spoken of a "knife fight to the finish" to wrestle the leadership from Juppe.
"Juppe and others like him want to keep control of the RPR as if nothing had happened but I'm going to kick the ant hill," he was quoted as saying.
The jockeying for power within the RPR was mirrored in the upper ranks of the centre-right Union for French Democracy (UDF), the RPR's partner in the former ruling coalition.
Three faction leaders, Francois Leotard, Francois Bayrou and Alain Madelin, all made statements indicating that the loose-knit grouping was on the verge of breaking up.

Madelin, France's leading exponent of radical, free-market economic policies, wants to set up what he calls a "real liberal movement", blaming the right's failure to adopt such policies for its defeat.
